docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: These are notes based on my three lectures at the Midrasha Mathematicae from October 2026 on the cov vs. pp problem in pcf theory. The notes expand the material presented on slides by adding proofs and discussions.

docs.title: Basic Notation
docs.text:
Let \(J\) be an ideal over a set \(A\).

  • \(J^+=\{X\subseteq A:X\notin J\}\) is the collection of \(J\)-positive subsets of \(A\).
  • \(J^*=\{X\subseteq A:A\setminus X\in J\}\) denotes the dual filter.
  • \(J\mathbin{\upharpoonright}B=\{X\subseteq A:X\cap B\in J\}\).
  • \(J+B=J\mathbin{\upharpoonright}(A\setminus B)\).

docs.title: Comparisons modulo an ideal
docs.text:
For ordinal-valued functions with domain \(A\),

\[ \begin{aligned} f<_J g &\iff \{a\in A:g(a)\le f(a)\}\in J,\\ \\ f\le_J g &\iff \{a\in A:g(a)<f(a)\}\in J. \end{aligned} \]

The definitions of \(=_J\) and \(\ne_J\) are similar.

docs.title: Reduced Products
docs.text:
Our basic object of study will be reduced products \(\prod A/J\) for \(A\) a set of regular cardinals and \(J\) an ideal on \(A\). We usually assume that \(A\) is progressive, which means \(|A|<|\min(A)|\).

We may also consider indexed products \(\prod_{i\in\Gamma}\lambda_i\), where \(\Gamma\) is some index set and \(\lambda_i\) is a regular cardinal. The reduced product makes sense if \(J\) is an ideal on \(\Gamma\), and we say that this is a small product if

\[ |\Gamma|<\min\{\lambda_i:i\in\Gamma\}. \]

These approaches are equivalent.

docs.title: True cofinality
docs.text:
Let \(A\) be a progressive set of regular cardinals, and let \(J\) be a proper ideal on \(A\). We say

\[ \operatorname{tcf}\left(\prod A/J\right)=\kappa \]

if \(\kappa\) is regular and there is a sequence \(\langle f_\alpha:\alpha<\kappa\rangle\subseteq\prod A\) such that

\[ \alpha<\beta<\kappa\implies f_\alpha<_J f_\beta, \]

and the sequence is cofinal:

\[ (\forall g\in\prod A)(\exists\alpha<\kappa)\quad g<_J f_\alpha. \]

We will try to ground our exposition in the notation of the Abraham and Magidor chapter in the Handbook of Set Theory. When we need to apply results of pcf theory, we rely on their work and generally point the reader to where the needed results can be found.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
The applications of pcf theory to cardinal arithmetic exploit a connection between two different versions of cofinality, one concerned with families of sets ordered by inclusion (such as the cofinality of \([\aleph_\omega]^{\aleph_0}\) ordered by \(\subseteq\)) and the other concerned with functions in infinite products ordered modulo an ideal on the index set (such as the cofinality of \(\prod_{n<\omega}\aleph_n\) modulo the finite ideal).

The idea is that questions about the cofinalities of families of sets can sometimes be translated into questions about cofinalities of reduced products, and in this latter arena the tools of pcf theory can be used to analyze the situation. With luck, the pcf analysis then sheds light on the original question.

This interaction is evident in the most famous theorem of pcf theory: Shelah's result on \(\aleph_{\omega_4}\). If we strip away conventional cardinal arithmetic and look at the pcf-theoretic heart of his result, we see there are two pieces:

  1. \(\operatorname{cf}\left([\aleph_\omega]^{\aleph_0}, \subseteq\right)=\max\operatorname{pcf}(\{\aleph_{n+1}:n<\omega\})\), and
  2. \(\max\operatorname{pcf}(\{\aleph_{n+1}:n<\omega\})<\aleph_{\omega_4}.\)

The second statement is the part that grabs peoples' attention because of the mysterious appearance of \(\omega_4\), but our notes are going to focus on a general version of the first statement: When can questions about covering families of sets be translated into questions about reduced products of regular cardinals? This is the heart of the cov vs. pp problem.

docs.title: The example of \(\aleph_\omega\).
docs.text:
To kick things off, we will sketch a proof of statement 1.

Theorem

\[\max\operatorname{pcf}(\{\aleph_{n+1}:n<\omega\}) = \operatorname{cf}\left([\aleph_\omega]^{\aleph_0},\subseteq\right).\]

Let \(\tau=\max\operatorname{pcf}(\{\aleph_{n+1}:n<\omega\})\) and let \(\eta=\operatorname{cf}\left([\aleph_\omega]^{\aleph_0},\subseteq\right)\).

docs.title: One direction
docs.text:
The inequality \(\tau\leq\eta\) is the easier of the two, so we dispose of it first. This part of the proof is quite flexible, and shows us how to pass from covering families to cofinal sets of functions.

Given a countable subset \(X\) of \(\aleph_\omega\), we define the function \(g_X\in\prod A\) by

\[ g_X(a)=\sup(X\cap a). \]

Now suppose \(\mathcal{X}\) is cofinal in \(([\aleph_\omega]^{\aleph_0},\subseteq)\). Given any function \(f\in \prod A\), there will be an \(X\in \mathcal{X}\) such that

\[ \{f(a)+1:a\in A\}\subseteq X. \]

But then

\[ a\in A\Longrightarrow f(a)< g_X(a), \]

and so the family \(\{g_X:X\in\mathcal{X}\}\) is (pointwise) cofinal in \(\prod A\). Since \(\max\operatorname{pcf}(A)\) is the minimum cardinality of a pointwise cofinal subset of \(\prod A\), we see \(\tau\leq\eta\). We will encounter variants of this argument a little later as this is a basic tool.

docs.title: The Other Direction
docs.text:
The reverse inequality is more difficult, and proving it here will provide us with a case study of another basic technique that involves internally approachable elementary submodels and their characteristic functions. This part of the argument is where we will use the fact that \(|A|<\omega_1<\min(A)\), as \(\omega_1\) will be the length of the chain of models we use. This may be a good time for the reader to take a look at Section 5 of Abraham–Magidor, Cardinal Arithmetic to remind themselves of the notation that we are borrowing.

Fix a sufficiently large regular \(\chi\) and work in \(\mathfrak A=(H(\chi),\in,<_\chi)\), with the Skolem functions given by the fixed well-order \(<_\chi\). For each \(\eta\in\operatorname{pcf}(A)\), fix a universal sequence \(\vec f^\eta=\langle f^\eta_\xi:\xi<\eta\rangle\) of functions in \(\prod A\) that is minimally obedient at cofinality \(\omega_1\). Let \(\vec f=\langle\vec f^\eta:\eta\in\operatorname{pcf}(A)\rangle\) be the resulting array.

Let \(Y\subseteq\lambda\) be countable. Choose an increasing continuous chain \(\langle N_i:i<\omega_1\rangle\) of countable elementary submodels of \(\mathfrak A\) with \(Y\subseteq N_0\) and \(\lambda,A,\omega_1,\vec f\in N_0\). Since \(A\) is countable, \(A\subseteq N_0\).

At each successor stage arrange that \(\langle N_j:j\leq i\rangle\in N_{i+1}\). In particular, \(i,N_i\in N_{i+1}\). The union \(N=\bigcup_{i<\omega_1}N_i\) is internally approachable of length \(\omega_1\), has size \(\aleph_1\), and contains \(\omega_1+1\) pointwise. Its characteristic function on \(A\) is defined by

\[ \operatorname{Ch}_N(\rho)=\sup(N\cap\rho)\qquad(\rho\in A). \]

For each \(\rho\in A\), the sequence \(\langle\sup(N_i\cap\rho):i<\omega_1\rangle\) is continuous and strictly increasing. Indeed, \(\sup(N_i\cap\rho)\) and its successor both belong to \(N_{i+1}\cap\rho\). The sequence is cofinal in \(\operatorname{Ch}_N(\rho)\). Consequently \(N\cap\rho\) contains a club in \(\operatorname{Ch}_N(\rho)\), and this ordinal has cofinality \(\omega_1\).

docs.title: Model comparison
docs.text:
We formulate the model comparison lemma for an arbitrary uncountable cardinal \(\lambda\) so that we can quote it later.

Model Comparison Lemma

Let \(\lambda\) be an uncountable cardinal and suppose \(M\) and \(N\) are elementary submodels of \(\mathfrak A\) with

\[ M\subseteq N \text{ and }\lambda\in M. \]

Let \(\eta<\lambda\) be an infinite cardinal, and assume

  1. \(M\cap\eta=N\cap\eta\).
  2. \(\sup(M\cap\rho)=\sup(N\cap\rho)\) for every regular cardinal \(\rho\in M\) with \(\eta<\rho\leq\lambda\).

Then \(M\cap\lambda=N\cap\lambda\).

Proof. Suppose \(\alpha\in(N\cap\lambda)\setminus M\). Since \(\lambda\in M\), we can choose a set \(X\in M\) of least possible cardinality such that \(\alpha\in X\subseteq\lambda\). Put \(\kappa=|X|\).

If \(\kappa\leq\eta\), take a bijection \(b\colon\kappa\to X\) in \(M\). Then \(b^{-1}(\alpha)\in N\cap\kappa\subseteq M\) by (1), so \(\alpha\in M\), a contradiction.

Put \(\rho=\operatorname{cf}(\kappa)\). By elementarity, \(\rho\in M\), and there is an increasing sequence \(\langle X_i:i<\rho\rangle\in M\) whose union is \(X\), with \(|X_i|<\kappa\) for every \(i<\rho\). By elementarity of \(N\), some \(i\in N\cap\rho\) satisfies \(\alpha\in X_i\).

If \(\rho\leq\eta\), take \(j=i\in M\) by (1). Otherwise, \(\rho\) is a regular cardinal in \(M\) with \(\eta<\rho\leq\lambda\), so (2) gives \(j\in M\cap\rho\) with \(i\leq j\). In either case, \(X_j\in M\) contains \(\alpha\) and has size less than \(\kappa\), contradicting the choice of \(X\). \(\square\)

docs.title: Back to our proof
docs.text:
Return to \(\lambda=\aleph_\omega\) and \(A=\{\aleph_n:2\leq n<\omega\}\). We use the Model Comparison Lemma to show that for an internally approachable model \(N\) as discussed above, the set \(N\cap\lambda\) is determined by the characteristic function of \(N\) on \(A\). Suppose \(N\) and \(N'\) are unions of towers as above with the same characteristic function on \(A\), and define \(M=N\cap N'\). Since the two models are closed under the same Skolem functions, \(M\prec\mathfrak A\).

Take \(\eta=\omega_1\). All three models contain \(\omega_1\) pointwise, and for each \(\rho\in A\) the traces \(N\cap\rho\) and \(N'\cap\rho\) contain clubs in their common supremum, which has cofinality \(\omega_1\). These clubs intersect cofinally, so

\[ \sup(M\cap\rho)=\sup(N\cap\rho)=\sup(N'\cap\rho). \]

The regular cardinals in \((\omega_1,\lambda]\) are exactly the members of \(A\). Apply the Model Comparison Lemma to \(M\subseteq N\) and to \(M\subseteq N'\). It follows that \(N\cap\lambda=N'\cap\lambda\).

The tower makes \(N\) \(\omega_1\)-presentable in the sense of Abraham–Magidor. By their Corollary 5.9, \(\operatorname{Ch}_N\) is the pointwise maximum of finitely many functions from the fixed array \(\vec f\). Since the array contains at most \(\max\operatorname{pcf}(A)\) functions, at most \(\max\operatorname{pcf}(A)\) characteristic functions occur. (See Abraham–Magidor, Cardinal Arithmetic, Definition 5.6 and Corollary 5.9.)

We can now choose one representative tower for each characteristic function that occurs. Every countable \(Y\subseteq\lambda\) is contained in the trace of the union of one of the representative towers. By regularity of \(\omega_1\), \(Y\) is already contained in the trace of a countable stage of that tower. Taking all the countable stages of the representative towers therefore gives a cofinal family in \(([\lambda]^{\aleph_0},\subseteq)\) of size at most \(\max\operatorname{pcf}(A)\cdot\aleph_1=\max\operatorname{pcf}(A)\).

docs.title: Representability
docs.text:
Let \(\lambda\) be a singular cardinal. A cardinal \(\kappa\) is representable at \(\lambda\) if there are a set \(A\) and an ideal \(J\) such that

  • \(A\) is cofinal in \(\lambda\cap\operatorname{Reg}\)
  • \(|A|=\operatorname{cf}(\lambda)\)
  • \(J\) is an ideal on \(A\) extending the bounded ideal \(J^{\mathrm{bd}}_A\)
  • \(\kappa = \operatorname{tcf}\left(\prod A/J\right)\)

docs.title: The pseudopower function
docs.text:
Now we define

\[\operatorname{PP}(\lambda)=\{\kappa:\kappa\text{ is representable at }\lambda\},\]

and

\[\operatorname{pp}(\lambda)=\sup\operatorname{PP}(\lambda).\]

\(\operatorname{pp}(\lambda)\) is called the pseudopower of \(\lambda\) and it functions as a pcf-theoretic version of the gimel function \(\gimel(\lambda)=\lambda^{\operatorname{cf}(\lambda)}\).

Note that \(\lambda^+\) is representable at \(\lambda\) by Shelah's theorem on the existence of scales, so \(\operatorname{pp}(\lambda)\geq\lambda^+\).

docs.title: Combinatorial Significance
docs.text:
What does the cardinal \(\operatorname{pp}(\lambda)\) really mean?

Given \(\delta<\lambda\) let \(R(\delta,\lambda)\) be the collection of regular cardinals in the interval \((\delta,\lambda)\). If \(\operatorname{cf}(\lambda)\leq\delta\) then any subset \(A\) of \(R(\delta,\lambda)\) of cardinality \(\operatorname{cf}(\lambda)\) will be progressive, and hence \(\max\operatorname{pcf}(A)\) will exist and it is equal to the pointwise cofinality of the product \(\prod A\).

If we define

\[\eta(\delta)=\sup\{\max\operatorname{pcf}(A):A\subseteq R(\delta,\lambda)\text{ and }|A|=\operatorname{cf}(\lambda)\}\]

then \(\delta\leq\varepsilon<\lambda\) implies \(\eta(\varepsilon)\leq\eta(\delta)\) and hence there is a \(\delta<\lambda\) for which the value of \(\eta(\delta)\) achieves its minimum. We claim that \(\operatorname{pp}(\lambda)\) is precisely this stabilizing value \(\eta(\delta)\), that is, that

\[\operatorname{pp}(\lambda)=\min\{\sup\{\max\operatorname{pcf}(A): A\subseteq R(\delta,\lambda)\text{ and }|A|=\operatorname{cf}(\lambda)\}:\delta<\lambda\}.\]

Note that in the above equation, the set \(A\) may very well be bounded below \(\lambda\). The point is that \(\lambda\) has a tail so that any set \(A\) of \(\operatorname{cf}(\lambda)\) regular cardinals drawn from that tail will satisfy \(\max\operatorname{pcf}(A)\leq\operatorname{pp}(\lambda)\).

The inequality \(\leq\) should be clear: if \(\kappa\) is representable at \(\lambda\) as \(\prod A/J\) for \(A\) and \(J\) as in the definition, then for any \(\delta<\lambda\) we may discard the bounded set \(A\cap \delta+1\) (as it is \(J\)) and see that \(\kappa\) is in \(\operatorname{pcf}(A\setminus(\delta+1))\).

For the reverse inequality, put \(\kappa=\operatorname{cf}(\lambda)\) and \(P=\operatorname{pp}(\lambda)\). Suppose toward a contradiction that \(\eta(\delta)>P\) for every \(\kappa\leq\delta<\lambda\).

Choose an increasing sequence \(\langle\delta_i:i<\kappa\rangle\) cofinal in \(\lambda\), with \(\delta_0\geq\kappa\). For each \(i<\kappa\), choose \(A_i\subseteq R(\delta_i,\lambda)\) such that

\[|A_i|=\kappa\qquad\text{and}\qquad\max\operatorname{pcf}(A_i)>P.\]

Let \(A=\bigcup_{i<\kappa}A_i\). Then \(A\) is progressive, \(|A|=\kappa\), and \(\sup A=\lambda\). Moreover, for every \(\delta<\lambda\),

\[\max\operatorname{pcf}\bigl(A\setminus(\delta+1)\bigr)>P,\]

since some \(A_i\) is contained in \(A\setminus(\delta+1)\).

These tail maxima are nonincreasing as \(\delta\) increases, so they eventually stabilize. Discarding a bounded initial segment of \(A\), we may therefore assume that

\[\eta=\max\operatorname{pcf}(A)=\max\operatorname{pcf}\bigl(A\setminus(\delta+1)\bigr)>P\]

for every \(\delta<\lambda\).

Let

\[I=J_{<\eta}[A]=\{B\subseteq A:\operatorname{pcf}(B)\subseteq\eta\}.\]

By the basic pcf theorem, there is a \(<_I\)-increasing cofinal sequence \(\langle f_\alpha:\alpha<\chi\rangle\) in \(\prod A\).

Let \(J\) be the ideal generated by \(I\) together with the bounded subsets of \(A\). This ideal is proper: otherwise, for some \(\delta<\lambda\) we would have

\[A\setminus(\delta+1)\in I,\]

contradicting the fact that this tail has maximum possible cofinality \(\eta\).

Since \(I\subseteq J\), the same sequence remains \(<_J\)-increasing and cofinal. Consequently,

\[\operatorname{tcf}\left(\prod A/J\right)=\eta.\]

But \(|A|=\operatorname{cf}(\lambda)\) and \(J\) contains every bounded subset of \(A\), so this witnesses that \(\chi\) is representable at \(\lambda\). Thus

\[\eta\leq\operatorname{pp}(\lambda)=P,\]

a contradiction.

Therefore \(\eta(\delta)\leq\operatorname{pp}(\lambda)\) for some \(\delta<\lambda\). Together with the preceding inequality, this proves the claimed characterization.

\[\tag*{$\square$}\]

docs.title: Note
docs.text: If \(\lambda\) is not a fixed point, then for all sufficiently large \(\delta<\lambda\) the set \(R(\delta,\lambda)\) is a progressive interval of regular cardinals, and we can apply pcf analysis in this setting. This is one reason we know so much more about cardinal arithmetic at non-fixed points, and why getting information when \(\lambda=\aleph_\lambda\) is more difficult.

docs.title: 1.4 General Representability
docs.text: There are a few natural ways to modify the definition of representability. We will look at a couple of them here.

docs.title: \(\theta\)-representability
docs.text:
Let \(\lambda\) be singular and \(\operatorname{cf}(\lambda)\leq\theta<\lambda\). A regular cardinal \(\chi>\lambda\) is \(\theta\)-representable at \(\lambda\) if there are a progressive set \(A\subseteq\lambda\cap\operatorname{Reg}\) with \(|A|\leq\theta\) and \(\sup A=\lambda\), and a proper ideal \(J\supseteq J_A^{\mathrm{bd}}\), such that \(\chi=\operatorname{tcf}(\prod A/J)\). Define

\[\operatorname{pp}_\theta(\lambda)=\sup\{\chi:\chi\text{ is }\theta\text{-representable at }\lambda\}.\]

Thus \(\operatorname{pp}(\lambda)=\operatorname{pp}_{\operatorname{cf}(\lambda)}(\lambda)\).

Every \(\theta\)-representation is also a \(\theta'\)-representation whenever \(\theta\leq\theta'<\lambda\), so \(\operatorname{pp}_\theta(\lambda)\leq\operatorname{pp}_{\theta'}(\lambda)\). Other variants of this notation should be given the obvious meaning, for example, we define

\[\operatorname{pp}_{<\lambda}(\lambda)=\sup\{\operatorname{pp}_\theta(\lambda):\operatorname{cf}(\lambda)\leq\theta<\lambda\}.\]

docs.title: \(\Gamma(\theta,\sigma)\)-representability
docs.text:
We can also consider imposing more conditions on the ideals we use for representations. For example, assume \(\aleph_0\le\sigma=\operatorname{cf}(\sigma)\le\operatorname{cf}(\mu)<\theta<\mu\) and we define \(\Gamma(\theta,\sigma)\) to be the class of proper \(\sigma\)-complete ideals on sets of cardinality \(<\theta\).

Given this, it makes sense to define \(\operatorname{PP}_{\Gamma(\theta,\sigma)}(\lambda)\) consists of all regular cardinals \(\kappa\) such that

\[\kappa=\operatorname{tcf}\left(\prod A/J\right),\]

where

\[A\subseteq\lambda\cap\operatorname{Reg},\qquad \sup A=\lambda,\qquad |A|<\theta,\]

and \(J\in\Gamma(\theta,\sigma)\) is an ideal on \(A\) extending \(J_A^{\mathrm{bd}}\). Thus, \(\operatorname{pp}_{\Gamma(\theta,\sigma)}(\lambda)\) is the supremum of all of the \(\Gamma(\theta,\sigma)\)-representable cardinals at \(\lambda\).

The restrictions on \(\sigma\) and \(\theta\) are natural: if \(\theta\leq\operatorname{\operatorname{cf}(\lambda)}\) then any set of cardinality \(<\theta\) will be bounded, and we must require \(\sigma\leq\operatorname{cf}(\lambda)\) because \(\lambda\) is a union of \(\operatorname{cf}(\lambda)\) many bounded sets.

Note that \(\operatorname{pp}_{\theta}(\lambda)=\operatorname{pp}_{\Gamma(\theta^+,\aleph_0)}(\lambda)\) in this notation, so we have introduced a more general setting.

Also note a scale of length \(\lambda^+\) at \(\lambda\) shows us that \(\lambda^+\) is ALWAYS \(\Gamma(\theta,\sigma)\)-representable for any relevant \(\sigma\) and \(\theta\), as the bounded ideal is \(\operatorname{cf}(\lambda)\)-complete and the support of the scale has cardinality \(\operatorname{cf}(\lambda)\). Thus

\[\operatorname{pp}_{\Gamma(\theta,\sigma)}(\lambda)\geq\lambda^+.\]

Finally, we have the following version of our characterization of pseudopowers in terms of pcf on tails. It is essentially the same proof, just keeping track of the way the representations are built.

Lemma

Suppose \(\lambda\) is singular and \(\aleph_0\leq\sigma\leq\operatorname{cf}(\lambda)<\theta<\lambda\), with \(\sigma\) and \(\theta\) regular. There is a \(\beta\) with \(\theta\leq\beta<\lambda\) such that every nonempty \(B\subseteq(\beta,\lambda)\cap\operatorname{Reg}\) of size less than \(\theta\) satisfies

\[ \sup\operatorname{pcf}_{\Gamma(\theta,\sigma)}(B)\leq \operatorname{pp}_{\Gamma(\theta,\sigma)}(\lambda). \]

Equivalently, each such \(B\) is the union of fewer than \(\sigma\) nonempty sets \(B_\alpha\) with \(\max\operatorname{pcf}(B_\alpha)\leq \operatorname{pp}_{\Gamma(\theta,\sigma)}(\lambda)\).

Proof. We use two elementary facts about a progressive set \(A\). For a cardinal \(\kappa\), if \(\operatorname{tcf}(\prod A/J)=\nu>\kappa\), then \(J_{\leq\kappa}[A]\subseteq J\). Conversely, if \(I\) is a proper ideal containing \(J_{\leq\kappa}[A]\), choose an \(I\)-positive \(X\subseteq A\) with \(\eta=\max\operatorname{pcf}(X)\) as small as possible. Then \(\eta>\kappa\), and minimality gives \(J_{<\eta}[X]\subseteq I\restriction X\). Hence the usual \(\eta\)-scale on \(X\) remains a scale modulo \(I\restriction X\).

Now proceed as in the ordinary case. If no cutoff works, choose counterexamples \(B_i\) above cofinally increasing cutoffs greater than \(\theta\), for \(i<\kappa=\operatorname{cf}(\lambda)\). Let \(J_i\) be a proper \(\sigma\)-complete ideal on \(B_i\) witnessing a true cofinality above \(P\). The union \(C=\bigcup_{i<\kappa}B_i\) has size less than \(\theta\). Define an ideal \(I\) on \(C\) by $$ X\in I\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad {i<\kappa:X\cap B_i\notin J_i}\text{ is bounded in }\kappa. $$ Then \(I\) is proper and \(\sigma\)-complete, contains the bounded subsets of \(C\), and contains \(J_{<P^+}[C]\) by the first fact. The second fact now gives a \(\Gamma(\theta,\sigma)\)-representation at \(\lambda\) above \(P\), a contradiction.

For the equivalent formulation, apply the second fact to the \(\sigma\)-completion of \(J_{<P^+}[B]\). If that completion were proper, it would give a \(\sigma\)-complete true cofinality above \(P\) on a subset of \(B\). Thus the completion contains \(B\), which is exactly the asserted union property. The first fact gives the converse. \(\square\)

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Covering numbers are a combinatorial tool for analyzing the structure of \(([\lambda]^{<\lambda},\subseteq)\) when \(\lambda\) is a cardinal.

Definition

The covering number \(\operatorname{cov}(\lambda,\kappa,\theta,\sigma)\) is the least size of a family

\[\mathcal{X}\subseteq[\lambda]^{<\kappa}\]

such that every \(a\in[\lambda]^{<\theta}\) is contained in the union of fewer than \(\sigma\) members of \(\mathcal{X}\).

docs.title: Easy facts
docs.text:
For fixed values of the other parameters,

  • \(\operatorname{cov}(\lambda,\kappa,\theta,\sigma)\) is weakly decreasing as \(\kappa\) or \(\sigma\) increases;
  • \(\operatorname{cov}(\lambda,\kappa,\theta,\sigma)\) is weakly increasing as \(\lambda\) or \(\theta\) increases.

docs.title: Identities and a pcf bound
docs.text:
Two easy observations:

\[\operatorname{cov}(\lambda,\kappa,\theta,\aleph_0)=\operatorname{cov}(\lambda,\kappa,\theta,2).\] \[\operatorname{cov}(\lambda,\kappa^+,\kappa^+,2)=\operatorname{cof}\bigl([\lambda]^\kappa,\subseteq\bigr).\]

docs.title: A connection to pseudopowers
docs.text:
The following result is a little deeper than the preceding observations. It tells us that covering numbers bound pseudopowers:

Theorem

If \(\aleph_0\leq\sigma\leq\operatorname{cf}(\lambda)<\theta<\lambda\), then

\[\operatorname{pp}_{\Gamma(\theta,\sigma)}(\lambda)\leq\operatorname{cov}(\lambda,\lambda,\theta,\sigma).\]

Proof. Let \(\mathcal{X}\subseteq[\lambda]^{<\lambda}\) witness the covering number. Suppose that \(\chi\) is \(\Gamma(\theta,\sigma)\)-representable at \(\lambda\), witnessed by a set \(A\subseteq\lambda\cap\operatorname{Reg}\) with \(|A|<\theta\) and \(\sup A=\lambda\), and a proper \(\sigma\)-complete ideal \(J\supseteq J_A^{\mathrm{bd}}\), so that

\[\chi=\operatorname{tcf}\left(\prod A/J\right).\]

We show that \(\chi\leq|\mathcal{X}|\). Otherwise, for each \(x\in\mathcal{X}\) define \(g_x\in\prod A\) by

\[g_x(a)=\begin{cases}\sup(x\cap a),&|x|<a,\\0,&a\leq|x|.\end{cases}\]

Regularity of \(a\) ensures that \(g_x(a)<a\). Since \(|\mathcal{X}|<\chi\), a scale of length \(\chi\) gives a function \(f\in\prod A\) such that \(g_x<_J f\) for every \(x\in\mathcal{X}\).

Now \(|\operatorname{ran}(f)|<\theta\), so there are \(\rho<\sigma\) and \(x_i\in\mathcal{X}\) for \(i<\rho\) such that

\[\operatorname{ran}(f)\subseteq\bigcup_{i<\rho}x_i.\]

For each \(i<\rho\), let \(B_i=\{a\in A:f(a)\in x_i\}\). If \(a\in B_i\) and \(a>|x_i|\), then \(f(a)\leq g_{x_i}(a)\). Consequently,

\[B_i\subseteq\bigl(A\cap(|x_i|+1)\bigr)\cup\{a\in A:f(a)\leq g_{x_i}(a)\}\in J.\]

But \(A=\bigcup_{i<\rho}B_i\), contradicting the \(\sigma\)-completeness and properness of \(J\). Thus \(\chi\leq|\mathcal{X}|\), and taking the supremum over all such representations proves the inequality. \(\square\)

docs.title: Reduction of covering numbers to singular cardinals
docs.text:
The following theorem is proved by elementary combinatorics. It shows us how general covering numbers are governed by their values when the first two components are the same singular cardinal.

Theorem

Assume \(\lambda>\kappa\ge heta>\sigma\), where \(\kappa\) is infinite and \(\sigma\) is either an infinite regular cardinal or \(2\). Then

\[ \operatorname{cov}(\lambda,\kappa, heta,\sigma) = \lambda+ \sup_{\substack{\kappa\le u\le\lambda\ \sigma\le\operatorname{cf}( u)< heta}} \operatorname{cov}( u, u, heta,\sigma). \]

Note that when computing \(\operatorname{cov}(\lambda,\kappa, heta,\sigma)\) using the above formula, the right side involves all singular cardinals from the interval \([\kappa,\lambda]\) whose cofinality is from the interval \([\sigma, heta)\). (The supremum of the empty set is understood to be \(0\).)

docs.title: Proof
docs.text:
Let \(\chi\) be the right side. First observe that

\[ \operatorname{cov}(\mu,\mu, heta,\sigma)\le\chi \qquad(\kappa\le\mu\le\lambda). ag{1} \]

For the relevant singular \(\mu\), this follows from the definition of \(\chi\). For the other \(\mu\), use a cofinal sequence of proper initial segments of \(\mu\). If \(\operatorname{cf}(\mu)\ge heta\), every subset of size \(< heta\) is contained in one of these initial segments. If \(\operatorname{cf}(\mu)<\sigma\), the entire sequence has length \(<\sigma\) and covers all of \(\mu\). Thus these other diagonal covering numbers are at most \(\mu\le\chi\).

We now prove by induction on cardinals \(\mu\le\lambda\) that there is a family

\[ \mathcal P_\mu\subseteq[\mu]^{<\kappa}, \qquad |\mathcal P_\mu|\le\chi, \]

such that every \(x\in[\mu]^{< heta}\) is covered by fewer than \(\sigma\) members of \(\mathcal P_\mu\).

For \(\mu<\kappa\), take \(\mathcal P_\mu=\{\mu\}\). For \(\mu\ge\kappa\), choose by (1) a family

\[ \mathcal D_\mu\subseteq[\mu]^{<\mu}, \qquad |\mathcal D_\mu|\le\chi, \]

witnessing the diagonal covering number. For each \(a\in\mathcal D_\mu\), the induction hypothesis, transported along a bijection between \(|a|\) and \(a\), gives a family

\[ \mathcal P_a\subseteq[a]^{<\kappa}, \qquad |\mathcal P_a|\le\chi, \]

covering every subset of \(a\) of size \(< heta\) by fewer than \(\sigma\) members. Set

\[ \mathcal P_\mu = igcup_{a\in\mathcal D_\mu}\mathcal P_a. \]

Its size is at most \(\chi\).

Given \(x\in[\mu]^{< heta}\), first cover \(x\) by \(<\sigma\) members \(a\) of \(\mathcal D_\mu\), and then cover each \(x\cap a\) by \(<\sigma\) members of \(\mathcal P_a\). Regularity of \(\sigma\), or \(\sigma=2\), ensures that altogether we used \(<\sigma\) members of \(\mathcal P_\mu\). This completes the induction and proves the upper bound.

Conversely, restricting any witness for \(\operatorname{cov}(\lambda,\kappa, heta,\sigma)\) to \( u\) gives

\[ \operatorname{cov}( u, u, heta,\sigma) \le \operatorname{cov}(\lambda,\kappa, heta,\sigma) \qquad(\kappa\le u\le\lambda). \]

Also, because \(\kappa<\lambda\), fewer than \(\lambda\) sets of size \(<\kappa\) cannot cover all the singletons of \(\lambda\). Hence the covering number is at least \(\lambda\), proving equality.

\[ ag*{$\square$}\]

docs.title: 1.7 The cov vs. pp Theorem
docs.text: Can we go the other direction and use pseudopowers to bound covering numbers? The answer is "yes" in many cases, and we'll take a look at what is known. We are going to start with Shelah's cov vs. pp theorem, which tells us that covering numbers and pseudopowers are closely related, and we have an exact match between the two provided we are working with countably complete covers and ideals.

docs.title: The cov vs. pp theorem (Singular Cardinals Version)
docs.text:
Theorem

If \(\aleph_0<\sigma=\operatorname{cf}(\sigma)\leq\operatorname{cf}(\lambda)<\theta<\lambda\), then

\[\operatorname{pp}_{\Gamma(\theta,\sigma)}(\lambda)=\operatorname{cov}(\lambda,\lambda,\theta,\sigma).\]

docs.title: The general cov vs. pp theorem
docs.text:
If we combine the above result with Lemma ? we obtain the following more general form of the cov vs pp theorem.

Theorem

If \(\aleph_0<\sigma=\operatorname{cf}(\sigma)\leq\operatorname{cf}(\lambda)<\theta<\lambda\) with \(\theta\leq\kappa\leq\lambda\) then

\[\operatorname{cov}(\lambda,\kappa,\theta,\sigma)+\lambda=\sup_{\substack{\kappa\leq\mu\leq\lambda\\\sigma\leq\operatorname{cf}(\mu)<\theta}}\operatorname{pp}_{\Gamma(\theta,\sigma)}(\mu)+\lambda.\]

If \(\kappa<\lambda\), then the \(+\lambda\) on the left can be omitted. We want to note how the parameters from the left side appear on the right: we are covering sets in \([\lambda]^{<\theta}\) with unions of \(<\sigma\) sets from a family \(\mathcal{P}\subseteq[\lambda]^{<\kappa}\). On the right side, \(\theta\) and \(\sigma\) appear in the types of representations we are allowing, while the supremum is taken over those singular cardinals in the interval \([\kappa,\lambda]\) for which representations using ideals from \(\Gamma(\theta,\sigma)\) makes sense.

The restriction to uncountable \(\sigma\) is unfortunate, because it means the above theorems shed no light on what occurs at cardinals of countable cofinality in general.

docs.title: 1.8 Non-fixed points
docs.text:
We will now take a look at a result of Shelah that shows us how we pcf theory can be deployed more effectively when dealing with singular cardinals \(\lambda<\aleph_\lambda\).

Theorem

Suppose \(\lambda\) is singular, \(\lambda<\aleph_\lambda\), and \(\operatorname{cf}(\lambda)\leq\theta<\lambda\). Then

\[\operatorname{cov}(\lambda,\lambda,\theta^+,2)=\operatorname{pp}_\theta(\lambda).\]

In particular,

\[\operatorname{cov}\bigl(\lambda,\lambda,\operatorname{cf}(\lambda)^+,2\bigr)=\operatorname{pp}(\lambda).\]

This result is from Cardinal Arithmetic, Chapter IX, Claim 3.7, and Cardinal arithmetic for skeptics, Theorem 5.7. We have tried to give a more straightforward presentation of the proof along the lines of Abraham and Magidor's handbook article.

docs.title: What's special about a non-fixed point?
docs.text:
The proof requires a little more pcf theory than we've assumed elsewhere. To start, we need the following (somewhat famous) result of Shelah that we quote as a black box.

Theorem

If \(A\) is a progressive interval of regular cardinals, then \(|\operatorname{pcf}(A)|<|A|^{+4}\).

The above theorem is crucial for us because we are working with singular \(\lambda\) such that \(\lambda<\aleph_\lambda\), because for any such \(\lambda\) there is a \(\delta<\lambda\) so that \((\delta,\lambda)\cap\mathsf{Reg}\) is a progressive interval of regular cardinals. The next easy lemma uses this fact.

Lemma

Suppose \(\lambda\) is singular, \(\lambda<\aleph_\lambda\), and \(\operatorname{cf}(\lambda)\leq\theta<\lambda\). There is a regular cardinal \(\delta\) with \(\theta<\delta<\lambda\) such that, for \(A=(\delta,\lambda)\cap\operatorname{Reg}\), we have

  1. \(|\operatorname{pcf}(A)|<\delta\), and
  2. \(\max\operatorname{pcf}(B)\leq\operatorname{pp}_\theta(\lambda)\) for every nonempty \(B\subseteq A\) of size at most \(\theta\).

Proof. As we observed earlier, we can choose \(\beta<\lambda\) so that (2) holds for every nonempty \(B\subseteq(\beta,\lambda)\cap\mathsf{Reg}\) of size at most \(\theta\).

Write \(\lambda=\aleph_\alpha\). Since \(\lambda\) is not a fixed point, \(\alpha<\lambda\). Put \(\kappa=|\alpha|\). Since \(\lambda\) is a limit cardinal we know \(\kappa^{+4}<\lambda\), and so we may choose a regular cardinal \(\delta\) with

\[\max\{\beta,\theta,\kappa^{+4}\}<\delta<\lambda.\]

Now \(A=(\delta,\lambda)\cap\operatorname{Reg}\) has size at most \(\kappa\), since every cardinal in \(A\) has index below \(\alpha\). Thus \(|A|\leq\kappa<\delta<\min A\), and Shelah's bound for progressive intervals of regular cardinals gives

\[|\operatorname{pcf}(A)|<|A|^{+4}\leq\kappa^{+4}<\delta.\]

This proves (1), and (2) follows from \(\beta<\delta\). \(\square\)

Put \(P=\operatorname{pp}_\theta(\lambda)\), and take \(\delta\) and \(A=(\delta,\lambda)\cap\operatorname{Reg}\) from the preceding lemma. Then

\[ |A|\leq|\operatorname{pcf}(A)|<\delta<\min A. \]

Fix an array \(\vec f=\langle\vec f^\eta:\eta\in\operatorname{pcf}(A)\rangle\), where each \(\vec f^\eta=\langle f^\eta_\xi:\xi<\eta\rangle\) is a universal sequence in \(\prod A\) that is minimally obedient at cofinality \(\delta\). The inequality \(|A|<\delta<\min A\) allows us to choose these sequences. Abraham–Magidor, Cardinal Arithmetic, §5.2, following Definition 5.6.

docs.title: The lower bound
docs.text: As in the \(\aleph_\omega\) example, a covering family gives a cofinal family in every reduced product \(\prod B/J\) used to compute \(P\). For each covering set \(X\), put \(g_X(a)=\sup(X\cap a)\) when \(a>|X|\) and \(g_X(a)=0\) otherwise. Given \(f\in\prod B\), choose \(X\) containing \(\{f(a)+1:a\in B\}\), a set of size at most \(\theta\). Then \(f(a)<g_X(a)\) on the tail above \(|X|\), so \(f<_J g_X\) since \(J\) contains the bounded subsets of \(B\). Taking the supremum over the representations gives \(P\leq\operatorname{cov}(\lambda,\lambda,\theta^+,2)\).

docs.title: Reading the characteristic function from the scales
docs.text:
For each \(\gamma<\lambda\) of cofinality \(\delta\), fix a club \(e_\gamma\) in \(\gamma\) of order type \(\delta\). Work in one sufficiently large Skolemized structure \(\mathfrak A\) on \(H(\chi)\), with \(\lambda,\delta,A,\vec f\), and the club sequence named.

Fix \(Y\in[\lambda]^{\leq\theta}\). Build an increasing continuous chain \(\langle N_i:i\leq\delta\rangle\) of elementary submodels with \(|N_i|<\delta\) for \(i<\delta\), with \(Y\cup\operatorname{pcf}(A)\subseteq N_0\), and with \(\langle N_j:j\leq i\rangle\in N_{i+1}\) for each \(i<\delta\). Its union \(N=N_\delta\) has size \(\delta\) and contains \(\delta+1\) pointwise, so it is \(\delta\)-presentable in the sense of Abraham–Magidor.

Put \(h=\operatorname{Ch}_N\restriction A\) and \(\gamma_\eta=\sup(N\cap\eta)\) for \(\eta\in\operatorname{pcf}(A)\). As in the argument at \(\aleph_\omega\), the stage suprema form a club in \(h(a)\) contained in \(N\cap a\), and \(\operatorname{cf}(h(a))=\delta\) for each \(a\in A\).

For each \(\eta\in\operatorname{pcf}(A)\), both \(\eta\) and \(\vec f\) belong to \(N_0\), so \(\vec f^\eta\in N\). Also \(\gamma_\eta<\eta\) because \(\eta\) is regular and \(|N|=\delta<\min A\leq\eta\). Abraham–Magidor then give \(f^\eta_{\gamma_\eta}\leq h\) pointwise on \(A\). Moreover, the agreement set

\[ C_\eta=\{a\in A:f^\eta_{\gamma_\eta}(a)=h(a)\} \]

is a generator for \(\eta\), so \(J_{\leq\eta}[A]=J_{<\eta}[A]+C_\eta\). Abraham–Magidor, Cardinal Arithmetic, §5.2, Lemmas 5.4, 5.7, and 5.8(1).

docs.title: Coding the coordinates needed for \(Y\)
docs.text:
For each \(a\in A\), the club in \(h(a)\) contained in \(N\cap a\) meets \(e_{h(a)}\) cofinally. Fix a function on \(N\) that, given \(a\in A\) and \(x\in N\cap a\), selects a point of \(N\cap e_{h(a)}\) above \(x\). Take \(M\prec N\) of size at most \(\theta\) containing \(Y\) pointwise and closed under this function. Then

\[ M\cap e_{h(a)}\text{ is cofinal in }M\cap a \qquad(a\in M\cap A). \]

Abraham and Magidor's Corollary 5.9 expresses \(h\) on all of \(A\) as a finite pointwise maximum of functions from the array. For the model comparison below, we will find a finite pointwise maximum \(g\) that agrees with \(h\) on \(M\cap A\) using only sequences of length at most \(P\).

Put \(B_0=M\cap A\). While \(B_n\) is nonempty, put

\[ \eta_n=\max\operatorname{pcf}(B_n), \qquad B_{n+1}=B_n\setminus C_{\eta_n}. \]

Since \(B_n\subseteq M\cap A\) has size at most \(\theta\), the tail bound gives \(\eta_n\leq P\). Since \(B_n\in J_{\leq\eta_n}[A]\) and \(C_{\eta_n}\) is a generator, \(B_{n+1}\in J_{<\eta_n}[A]\). Thus \(\eta_{n+1}<\eta_n\) whenever \(B_{n+1}\) is nonempty, so the process terminates after finitely many steps.

Let \(g\) be the pointwise maximum of the finitely many selected functions \(f^{\eta_n}_{\gamma_{\eta_n}}\). Each is pointwise at most \(h\), and at every coordinate in \(M\cap A\) at least one of them equals \(h\). Hence \(g=h\) on \(M\cap A\).

Let \(\mathcal G\) consist of all finite pointwise maxima of functions \(f^\eta_\xi\) with \(\eta\in\operatorname{pcf}(A)\) and \(\xi<\eta\leq P\). The finite list of pairs \((\eta_n,\gamma_{\eta_n})\) determines \(g\) on all of \(A\). There are at most \(P\) possible pairs, and hence at most \(P\) finite lists. Thus \(g\) lies in a family \(\mathcal G\) of size at most \(P\) fixed independently of \(Y\).

docs.title: Applying model comparison
docs.text:
Let

\[ L=\operatorname{Hull}_{\mathfrak A}\bigl((\delta+1)\cup\{g\}\bigr), \qquad K=M\cap L. \]

The common Skolem functions give \(K\prec\mathfrak A\), and \(\delta\subseteq L\) gives \(K\cap\delta=M\cap\delta\).

Let \(a\in K\) be regular with \(\delta<a\leq\lambda\). Since \(\lambda\) is singular, \(a\in A\), so \(a\in M\cap A\) and \(h(a)=g(a)\in L\). Hence \(e_{h(a)}\in L\). Its increasing enumeration has domain \(\delta\), so \(\delta\subseteq L\) gives \(e_{h(a)}\subseteq L\). Therefore \(K\cap a\) contains \(M\cap e_{h(a)}\), which is cofinal in \(M\cap a\).

Apply the Model Comparison Lemma to \(K\subseteq M\) with cutoff \(\delta\). We obtain

\[ Y\subseteq M\cap\lambda=K\cap\lambda\subseteq L\cap\lambda. \]

As \(g\) ranges over \(\mathcal G\), the traces of these hulls give at most \(P\) sets of size at most \(\delta\) covering \([\lambda]^{\leq\theta}\). Together with the lower bound, this yields

\[ P =\operatorname{cov}(\lambda,\lambda,\theta^+,2) =\operatorname{cov}(\lambda,\delta^+,\theta^+,2). \]

  1. Saharon Shelah, Cardinal Arithmetic, Oxford Logic Guides 29, Oxford University Press, 1994. See Chapter II for generators and covering calculus, and Chapter IX, Sections 2–3, especially Claim 3.7 and its proof.

  2. Saharon Shelah, “Cardinal arithmetic for skeptics,” Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society (N.S.) 26 (1992), 197–210. Theorem 5.7, p. 204. PDF.

docs.title: 1.9 The cov vs pp problem
docs.text:
We have seen two theorems tying together covering numbers and pseudopowers.

Shelah's cov vs. pp theorem says that there is an exact match, provided we are allowed to use countable unions in our attempts to cover:

Theorem

If \(\aleph_0<\sigma=\operatorname{cf}(\sigma)\leq\operatorname{cf}(\lambda)<\theta<\lambda\) with \(\theta\leq\kappa\leq\lambda\) then

\[\operatorname{cov}(\lambda,\kappa,\theta,\sigma)+\lambda=\sup_{\substack{\kappa\leq\mu\leq\lambda\\\sigma\leq\operatorname{cf}(\mu)<\theta}}\operatorname{pp}_{\Gamma(\theta,\sigma)}(\mu)+\lambda.\]

If we drop that requirement, then we have an exact match when dealing with cardinals that are not fixed points:

Theorem

Suppose \(\lambda\) is singular, \(\lambda<\aleph_\lambda\), and \(\operatorname{cf}(\lambda)\leq\theta<\lambda\). Then

\[\operatorname{cov}(\lambda,\lambda,\theta^+,2)=\operatorname{pp}_\theta(\lambda).\]

In particular,

\[\operatorname{cov}\bigl(\lambda,\lambda,\operatorname{cf}(\lambda)^+,2\bigr)=\operatorname{pp}(\lambda).\]
